## Introduction

The N400 is a negative-going event-related potential (ERP) component elicited by meaningful stimuli, most frequently words, and it is sensitive to how well a stimulus fits its semantic context [@Kutas_ThirtyYearsCounting_2011]. Its polarity is negative and typically begins around 200 to 250 ms after stimulus onset and peaks at about 400 ms and returns toward baseline by 500 to 600 ms [@junge_DevelopmentN400Word_2021]. The topography is centro-parietal, with the largest amplitudes at midline sites such as Cz and Pz and typically a right-hemisphere bias is observed for words presented visually [@Kutas_ThirtyYearsCounting_2011]. Based on this, @kappenman_ERP_CORE_2021 measured the N400 at the centro-parietal midline electrode CPz, in a 300 to 500 ms window. They quantified it as a difference wave, where the N400 effect is the more negative response to semantically unrelated words compared with related words.

### Literature Review

The N400 was first reported by @kutas_ReadingSenselessSentences_1980, when a sentence reading task showed that words that were physically larger than normal elicited a late positive series of potentials, compared to semantically inappropriate words that elicited a late negative wave (N400). Further observation showed the effect was not simply a response to surprise or physical deviance, when unexpected words in a physically larger font elicited a late positivity instead. Subsequently, @kutas_ReadingSenselessSentences_1980 indicated that the N400 is specifically linked to meaning. A follow-up study by @kutas_BrainPotentialsReading_1984 then showed that N400 amplitude changes inversely with a word’s cloze probability, the amount of people who would complete the sentence with that word, therefore, the N400 component is graded rather than all-or-none anomaly detector.

@bentin_EventrelatedPotentialsLexical_1985 found that N400 is not limited to sentences. Participants were asked to judge whether a target word was related to the preceding prime, and a larger N400 was observed for unrelated rather than related word pairs, which adheres to the logic of the paradigm. The component occurs in response to essentially all meaningful or potentially meaningful stimuli, including linguistic cues like written words or spoken language, and non-linguistic stimuli like faces, and pictures [@junge_DevelopmentN400Word_2021]. The amplitude is reduced by semantic association, supportive context, higher word frequency, and repetition [@Kutas_ThirtyYearsCounting_2011]. The N400 is not an indicator of anomaly, but rather a general signature of semantic processing, with larger amplitudes seen when a stimulus is difficult to retrieve from memory based on context.

There is widespread agreement that the N400 reflects the processing of meaning, but the specific mechanism has been debated. @lauCorticalNetworkSemantics2008 stated that it reflects access to or retrieval of stored semantic information from long-term memory (LTM), which is altered and facilitated by context. However, another account holds that it reflects the integration of a word’s meaning into the ongoing context [@hagoortIntegrationWordMeaning2004]. More recently, a combination of both accounts has been proposed, known as the Lexical Retrieval View. Under this model, the amplitude of the N400 does not reflect the result of the words combining solely, it assigns lexical retrieval to the N400 and the later integration of meaning into a sentence representation to the P600 [@aurnhammer_RetrievalN400Integration_2021].

### Controversies

The N400 has several controversies surrounding its specifics. First, the role of prediction is contested. Some studies reported that N400 amplitudes reflects pre-activation of specific upcoming words [@delongProbabilisticWordPreactivation2005], but a multi-lab replication trial by @nieuwland_LargescaleReplicationStudy_2018 did not replicate the original effect. Second, the retrieval versus integration discussion is contentious, and the two accounts make different predictions for how stimulus properties and context should impact amplitude. Third, sentences that are implausible but contain a semantically related word, referred to as semantic illusion, can elicit a P600 rather than an N400, which opposes the account that the N400 is a signal of semantic anomaly and consolidates the understand that it is a signature of semantic processing [@kuperberg_NeuralMechanismsLanguage_2007]. Finally, the N400 overlaps in time with other components, and interferes with and is influenced by neighbouring component and by task demands, ultimately altering the measured effects. These issues can be observed in ERP CORE through the explicit relatedness judgement, and highlight the limitations on what simple related versus unrelated contrast can truly show about the underlying mechanism.

## Methods

The data analysed here come from the ERP CORE resource [@kappenman_ERP_CORE_2021], which is shared under a Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0) licence. The N400 dataset was used in a slightly modified format provided for this unit.

### Participants

The ERP CORE sample consisted of 40 neurotypical participants (25 females, 15 males; mean age 21.5 years, *SD* = 2.87, range 18 to 30; 38 right-handed and 2 left-handed) from the University of California, Davis community [@kappenman_ERP_CORE_2021]. All participants had native English competence and normal colour perception, normal or corrected-to-norma vision, and no self-reported history of neurological disease or injury. The study was approved by the UC Davis Institutional Review Board and informed consent was provided. Participants received $10 per hour throughout the trial.

In the original study, participants were excluded from a given task if artifacts affected more than 25% of trials, if fewer than 50% of trials remained in any single condition, or if accuracy was below 75% [@kappenman_ERP_CORE_2021]. For the N400, this resulted in 39 participants. In the present analysis, the sample was reduced to 38, with two participants (030 and 040) being excluded from the full sample. Participant 040 was removed as over 25% of trials were rejected due to artifact and less than 50% of trials remained after artifact rejection. For, Participant 030, the rejection conditions meant 314 of 362 epochs were dropped, leaving 1 related and 0 unrelated target epochs. Large blink artifacts are the cause of these rejections, but @kappenman_ERP_CORE_2021 corrected blinks through Independent Component Analysis(ICA), and this pipeline does not. The final sample therefore comprised 38 participants (24 females, 14 males; mean age 21.5, *SD* = 2.94, range 18 to 30; 36 right-handed and 2 left-handed).

```{python}
# Participants to exclude based on artifacts
EXCLUDE = ["030", "040"]
```

### Procedure

The N400 was elicited with a word pair judgement task adapted from @holcomb_AuditoryVisualSemantic_1990. On each trial, a red prime word was presented followed by a green target word, and participants responded by a button press depending on if the target word was semantically related or unrelated to the prime. For example, CAR followed by TRUCK is a related pair, and BANANA followed by KEYBOARD is an unrelated pair. Each target word was presented twice during the task, once preceded by an associated prime and once by an associated prime, with the order being full randomised. The number of trials per condition was 60 for related and unrelated word pairs, meaning the total number of trials was 120. The stimulus for the prime and target word was equal at 200 ms, and an average of 1000ms was provided between words and 1500ms between trials. The task was run in 1 continuous block of 120 trials with participants afforded a short break every 20 trials within that block. Trials with reaction times outside 200 to 1500 ms after target onset, or incorrect  responses, were excluded in the original analysis. 

### EEG recording

The continuous EEG was recorded with a BioSemi ActiveTwo system using active electrodes. Thirty scalp electrodes were mounted in an elastic cap and placed according to the International 10/20 system (FP1, F3, F7, FC3, C3, C5, P3, P7, P9, PO7, PO3, O1, Oz, Pz, CPz, FP2, Fz, F4, F8, FC4, FCz, Cz, C4, C6, P4, P8, P10, PO8, PO4, O2). The common mode sense (CMS) electrode was at PO1 and the driven right leg (DRL) electrode at PO2. The horizontal EOG was recorded from electrodes lateral to the external canthus of each eye, and the vertical EOG from an electrode below the right eye. Signals were low-pass filtered with a fifth-order sinc filter (half-power cutoff 204.8 Hz) and digitised at 1024 Hz with 24-bit resolution. All signals were recorded in single-ended mode, meaning references was done offline. The filtering for the present analysis on N400 is described below.

### Analysis parameters

#### Preprocessing parameters

Following @kappenman_ERP_CORE_2021, the EEG was re-referenced offline to the average of P9 and P10, due to their proximity to the mastoids. The data were band-pass filtered between 0.1 Hz and 30 Hz.

```{python}

FILTER_SETTINGS = {
    "low_cutoff": 0.1,
    "high_cutoff": 30.0
}

# This setting re-references to averaged mastoids (P9/P10 as proxy) 
REFERENCE = ["P9","P10"]

```

#### Epoching parameters

The parameters utilised here for the N400 mimic those specified by @kappenman_ERP_CORE_2021. The stimulus-locked epochs from -200 ms to 800 ms with a baseline of -200 to 0 ms, measured at CPz (specified later). The epochs were averaged separately for the related and unrelated target-word conditions, and when the EEG exceeded ±150 µV or the EOG exceeded ±250 µV they were rejected.

```{python}
TMIN = -0.2 # epoch start relative to critical event
TMAX = 0.8  # epoch end relative to critical event

BASELINE = (-0.2,0) # baseline interval

# critical conditions for averaging and epoching relevant to N400 component
CONDITIONS = ["stimulus/target_word/related", "stimulus/target_word/unrelated"]

REJECT = {
    "eeg": 150e-6,
    "eog": 250e-6
}

```

## Data analysis

### Preprocessing

Each participant's raw EEG file was downloaded and passed through a custom preprocessing function. The functions re-referenced the data to the average of P9 and P10 and applied a 0.1 to 30 Hz band-pass filter, following the parameters outlined previously. The preprocessed recordings were saved into a seperate folder to avoid the process repeating every run.

```{python}
#| eval: true # set this to false if you don't want preprocessing to recompute
#| output: false # this suppresses any output

for raw_file in RAW_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz"):

    # extract subject number
    subj_ID = raw_file.stem.split("_")[0]

    # read in raw file 
    raw = SimpleRaw(raw_file)

    # preprocess raw file
    # note how we draw on a custom preprocessing function here
    processed = preprocess(raw, 
                            reref_params = REFERENCE, 
                            filter_low_cutoff = FILTER_SETTINGS["low_cutoff"], 
                            filter_high_cutoff = FILTER_SETTINGS["high_cutoff"])
    
    processed.save(PROCESSED_PATH / f"{subj_ID}_raw.fif.gz", overwrite = True)


```

### Epoching and averaging

The preprocessed files were loaded for each participant, outside of the two excluded (030 and 040). Events were extracted from each recording, and the continuous data was cut into epochs as per the parameters mentioned previously.

```{python}
#| output: false

# initialise empty dictionary to hold single-subject averages
ss_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:
    ss_avs[cond] = []

for processed_file in PROCESSED_PATH.glob("*_raw.fif.gz"):
    
    # extract subject number
    subj_ID = processed_file.stem.split("_")[0]

    # check if participant should be excluded
    if subj_ID in EXCLUDE:
        # if participant is in list skip the rest for this participant
        # and move onto the next
        continue

    # read in preprocessed file
    processed = SimpleRaw(processed_file)

    # extract events
    events, event_id = processed.get_events()

    # epoch data
    epochs = SimpleEpoch(processed, events, event_id, tmin = TMIN, tmax = TMAX, baseline = BASELINE, reject = REJECT)

    # subset epochs and average by condition 
    for cond in CONDITIONS:
        av = epochs[cond].average()
        ss_avs[cond].append(av)

```

### Grand average

The single-participant averages were then averaged across the 38 included participants, providing one grand-average ERP per condition for plotting.

```{python}
#| output: false

# create an empty dict to hold our grand averages
grand_avs = {}

for cond in CONDITIONS:
    grand = grand_average(ss_avs[cond])
    grand_avs[cond] = grand
```

## Results

### Grand average: expected effect

At CPz, unrelated target words elicited a response more negative-going than the related target words, beginning around 250 to 300 ms and continuing through the 300 to 500 ms analysis window. Negative is plotted upwards. Dash vertical lines mark the analysis window of 300 to 500 ms recommended by @kappenman_ERP_CORE_2021.

```{python}
selected_electrode = "CPz"
plot_title = "Grand average ERPs at CPz (N = 38)"
analysis_window_start = 0.3
analysis_window_end = 0.5

plot_evokeds(grand_avs, picks = selected_electrode, invert_y = True, title = plot_title, vlines = [analysis_window_start, analysis_window_end])


```

## Discussion and reflection

The grand average at CPz showed the expected N400 semantic relatedness effect. From around 300 ms after target onset, unrelated words elicited a more negative-going waveform than related words, and the two waveforms remained separated through the 300 to 500 ms analysis window. Based on the plot, the difference was roughly 6 to 8 µV, which aligns with @kappenman_ERP_CORE_2021, who reported a mean N400 difference-wave amplitude of around -7.6 µV at CPz. The polarity, timing and electrode side of the effect were therefore replicated, however, this comparison is limited because the two waveforms are plotted individually rather than the unrelated-minus-related difference wave that ERP CORE displayed. There was a difference in the pipelines utilised. The fixed rejection threshold and a 30 Hz low-pass filter was used which did not mirror the ERP CORE. There was also only 38 participants used rather than 39 participants due to the rejection artifacts. Any of these changes could alter the absolute amplitudes.

Applying the pipeline to a new dataset has taught me how much depends on the specific parameters relevant to each component. My first attempt at using this pipeline for the N400 I tried the tags stimulus/related and stimulus/unrelated, which meant the prime words were being matched also. This caused mixed trials and did not provide any relevant information. I think showed to me how useful an open and collaborative space would be in the field of coding, because through a few small alterations (which would take less time the more I would do it) I was able to replicate this pipeline for an entirely new set of data and participants. I found this process extremely rewarding and thought-provoking because it challenged me to think and try troubleshoot errors based on the traceback.
